title: How Can You Use Inito After Ovulation? A Guide to Track Your Luteal Phase with Inito
summary: Learn how to track your luteal phase with Inito, confirm ovulation, understand PdG trends, luteal phase length, and PMS symptoms for better fertility insights.
body_text: The luteal phase can be a confusing time. Many symptoms overlap, it’s easy to overanalyze every change, and the two-week wait can make it difficult to know what’s actually happening in your body. Here’s how you can use Inito to better understand your luteal phase and what your hormone patterns may be telling you. Disclaimer: Inito is a fertility monitor that helps you track and confirm ovulation and gives you insights into your unique cycle and hormone trends. It is not designed to detect or monitor implantation or pregnancy. Key Takeaways The luteal phase refers to the second half of your cycle after ovulation. Luteal phase length usually falls between 12-14 days, but some variation is normal. A steady and consistent increase in PdG helps confirm ovulation. Progesterone and its urine metabolite PdG typically rise a few days after ovulation and peak around 6-8 DPO. A consistently short luteal phase (<11 days) may point to an underlying issue. Tracking DPO helps you better interpret symptoms and time pregnancy tests accurately. Many early symptoms overlap, making hormone trends more reliable than guesswork. Taking a pregnancy test early can lead to unnecessary confusion and false negatives. Tracking symptoms alongside hormones helps you understand your unique patterns. What is the luteal phase? The luteal phase is the latter half of your menstrual cycle: the time after ovulation and before your next period begins. It typically lasts 12-14 days , and during this phase, progesterone becomes the dominant hormone. Its role is to prepare your uterine lining for a possible pregnancy by making it thicker and more supportive for implantation. If pregnancy doesn’t occur, progesterone levels drop, and your period begins, marking the end of the luteal phase. Know more: Luteal Phase: All the Science, Simplified What hormones does Inito measure in the luteal phase? Inito measures four key fertility hormones during the luteal phase (and throughout the rest of your cycle as well): FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) LH (luteinizing hormone) E3G (urine metabolite of estrogen) PdG (urine metabolite of progesterone) While all four continue to be measured after ovulation, each hormone plays a different role during the luteal phase. FSH : FSH remains at low levels during the luteal phase because its primary job (stimulating follicle growth for that cycle) is complete. Occasionally, it may rise to support corpus luteum function or to help prepare for the next menstrual cycle. Estrogen: Although estrogen is often associated with the follicular phase, it continues to play an important role after ovulation. Many people experience a second, smaller rise in estrogen in the luteal phase (specifically, the mid-luteal phase), which works alongside progesterone to support the uterine lining. LH: LH after ovulation typically fall back toward baseline. Tracking LH alongside your other hormones provides context for when ovulation occurred and helps you better understand your overall hormone pattern. It can also help boost the functioning of the corpus luteum. PdG (urine metabolite of progesterone): After ovulation, the corpus luteum begins producing progesterone. In urine, this is measured as PdG. PdG tracking with Inito helps confirm ovulation. By tracking all four hormones together, Inito provides a more complete picture of what’s happening during the luteal phase. Know more: What Your Hormone Chart Reveals About Your Cycle How can you track your luteal phase with Inito? Here’s how you can use Inito in your luteal phase: 1. Confirm ovulation (not just predict it) One of the most important things Inito helps you do is confirm that ovulation actually happened. Ovulation predictor kits (OPKs) detect LH, which rises before ovulation. But LH alone can only predict ovulation; it cannot confirm that the egg was released. That’s where PdG (a urine metabolite of progesterone) comes in. PdG rises soon after ovulation . It can take a few days to increase and typically peaks around 6-8 days past ovulation (DPO). Tracking a steady and consistent rise in PdG is key because it confirms that your body has released an egg and successfully transitioned into the luteal phase. Why this matters: Anovulation (when ovulation doesn’t occur) is the leading cause of infertility. Around 25-30% of female infertility cases are linked to not ovulating. It often goes unnoticed without hormone tracking. 2. Track your luteal phase length Your luteal phase length is a critical but often overlooked fertility marker. The typical luteal phase range is 12-14 days, although it can vary between 11-17 days . In a study involving over 600,000 cycles, researchers found that the mean luteal phase length was actually 12.4 days . A short luteal phase is defined as ≤11 days (this includes the day of ovulation). Why this matters: A consistently short luteal phase may indicate a luteal phase defect (LPD), a condition where the body either: Doesn’t produce enough progesterone, or Doesn’t respond to progesterone effectively Research shows: 13% of ovulatory cycles have a luteal phase <10 days 18% of cycles have a luteal phase <12 days 35% of early pregnancy loss and ~4% of recurrent pregnancy loss are linked to luteal insufficiency So, when progesterone support is inadequate, the uterine lining may not develop enough for implantation or may struggle to maintain a pregnancy. Take a look at this Inito hormone chart after ovulation, where the luteal phase is about 10 days long: If you notice that your luteal phase is spanning less than 11 days consistently across cycles, discuss with your healthcare provider to better understand what your body might need. Note: Inito can help you understand your hormone patterns, but it can’t diagnose medical conditions or confirm pregnancy. Tracking your luteal phase length across multiple cycles can provide helpful context for discussions with your healthcare provider. Know more: How to Lengthen the Luteal Phase? Fertility’s Game-Changer! 3. Know exactly how many DPO you are Once ovulation is confirmed, Inito tracks your Days Past Ovulation (DPO) accurately. This might seem like a small detail, but it changes how you interpret your entire luteal phase. Why this matters: Symptom clarity: For example, spotting around 8-10 DPO might feel like an early period, but it could also be implantation-related. Know more: PMS vs Pregnancy Symptoms You Should Know Better testing decisions: Nearly 41% of women take pregnancy tests too early (more than 4 days before their expected period). What’s more, those who test very early are over 5x more likely to get a negative result before eventually testing positive–simply because it’s too soon. So, testing earlier in the luteal phase is far more likely to give you a negative–even in cycles that may later turn positive. Waiting just a few extra days can significantly improve how reliable your result is. That’s why knowing your DPO matters. It helps you time your test better and avoid unnecessary stress and confusion. Know more: How Soon After Ovulation Can You Test for Pregnancy? 4. Track symptoms alongside hormone trends Your luteal phase isn’t just about hormones; it’s about how those hormones show up in your daily life. With Inito, you can correlate your luteal phase hormone patterns to your symptoms: Mood changes Energy levels Sleep patterns Physical symptoms like bloating or cramps Over time, this helps you: Spot patterns unique to your body Anticipate PMS or luteal-phase shifts Proactively adjust your nutrition, workouts, and rest based on your luteal phase patterns In the long term, instead of just reacting to symptoms, you can start preparing for them. Know more: Cycle Syncing: What it Is and How to Start When you look at it together, here’s what you’re tracking and how each of these helps you better understand your cycle: What you’re tracking Why it matters Ovulation confirmation Confirms that egg release actually happened Luteal phase length If your luteal phase is consistently shorter than 11 days, it’s worth talking to your doctor Days Past Ovulation (DPO) Can help guide testing decisions and symptom interpretation Hormone trends + symptoms Helps you understand your unique patterns What if your luteal phase looks different? Not every cycle will look the same, and that’s expected. Hormones can fluctuate from cycle to cycle. However, some patterns are worth paying closer attention to: No confirmed ovulation for 2-3 cycles Luteal phase consistently less than 11 days Severe symptoms that interfere with daily life (PMS or PMDD-like patterns) These trends don’t automatically mean something is wrong. But they can be helpful signals to discuss with a healthcare provider. Know more: What Your Hormone Chart Reveals About Your Cycle What if I’m on progesterone supplements? Will Inito still be helpful? If you’re taking progesterone supplements, it’s important to understand how they can affect your results. Progesterone supplements can influence your PdG levels. If you’re PdG tracking with Inito, remember that Inito cannot differentiate between progesterone coming from a supplement and what your body is producing naturally. So, if PdG starts rising after you begin a supplement, it may reflect the supplement rather than your body’s own hormone production, which can give you a false positive result. That’s why it’s generally recommended to start progesterone supplements only after ovulation has been confirmed . (Although if you’ve been prescribed progesterone supplements, it’s best to have a conversation with your doctor to know when to start taking them.) Note: Inito has not been tested for use with progesterone supplements. You cannot use it to track the efficacy of your supplements or manage your dosage. Take the example below. These charts compare two cycles from the same user. Even though she was taking progesterone supplements in one cycle, her PdG levels actually trended lower than they did in a cycle without supplements. Know more: A Comprehensive Guide to Progesterone Supplements What if your PdG isn’t rising enough in the luteal phase? If your PdG rise seems delayed, trends lower than expected, or is inconsistent, it can feel concerning. But here are a few things to keep in mind: PdG doesn’t rise instantly. It can take a few days after your LH surge to confirm ovulation. Hormones are released in pulses, so day-to-day variation can happen. Inito measures PdG, which is the urine metabolite of progesterone. Hydration, urine concentration, and timing of testing can all have an effect on PdG values. So, instead of focusing on a single value, look for a steady and consistent increase over multiple days. Know more: PdG Results on Inito Explained: Waiting for Rise, Rising, Confirmed, or Unlikely? And if you consistently notice that PdG does not rise across multiple cycles, or you feel that your PdG levels seem to trend low, it’s worth discussing with your doctor. What should you do during your luteal phase? Here are a few things to keep in mind during the luteal phase: Avoid testing too early The two-week wait (TWW) can feel long, but testing too early often leads to unnecessary confusion. Waiting until closer to your expected period can give you more reliable results. While some pregnancy tests can give you results from as early as 4 days before your tentative period (around 10 DPO ), it is best to take a pregnancy test until after your missed period . Know more: Your Complete Guide to Surviving the Two Week Wait Support your body with balanced habits Your luteal phase is a time when your body is naturally shifting toward rest and recovery. Moderate exercise (like walking, yoga, strength training) Balanced nutrition (focus on whole foods, stable energy) Adequate rest and sleep These can help you feel more stable during this phase. Know more: Best Foods to Eat During the Luteal Phase Build awareness, not anxiety The goal of tracking isn’t to overanalyze every symptom. It’s to build awareness over time and understand your patterns, not to react to every fluctuation. Find support when you need it Whether it’s a partner, the Inito community , or a guided program, having support during the luteal phase can make a big difference, especially during the TWW. Hearing from others on a similar journey, sharing experiences, or simply knowing you’re not alone can make this phase feel more manageable. Sometimes, just understanding what’s happening in your body is enough to ease uncertainty. Summary The luteal phase doesn’t have to feel like a guessing game. With Inito, you can: Confirm whether ovulation actually happened Understand your luteal phase length Track DPO accurately Correlate hormone patterns and symptoms Over time, this turns confusion into clarity and helps you make more informed decisions about your cycle. FAQs 1. Should I continue using Inito after ovulation? You can. While further testing is optional once ovulation is confirmed, many users continue testing during the luteal phase to track their hormone trends after ovulation. 2. Why does Inito keep asking me to test after ovulation? Inito asks you to keep testing after Peak Fertility to confirm if ovulation has actually happened. A steady and consistent rise in PdG confirms egg release. Continuing to test is helpful to track this PdG rise or, in case you experience another LH surge later in your cycle, Inito helps you catch that rise as well. 3. What hormones does Inito measure during the luteal phase? Inito continues to measure FSH, LH, estrogen, and PdG during your luteal phase. During this phase, PdG is especially important for confirming ovulation, while the other hormones provide additional context about your cycle. 4. Why are my hormone levels changing after ovulation? Hormones naturally continue to fluctuate during the luteal phase. For example, PdG rises after ovulation and estrogen may have a second, smaller rise as well. Day-to-day variation is expected, so it’s more helpful to look at overall trends than individual values. 5. Can I stop testing once ovulation is confirmed? Once ovulation is confirmed, further testing is optional. Some users choose to stop testing for that cycle, while others continue to track hormone trends throughout the luteal phase. 6. Why didn't my PdG rise immediately after ovulation? PdG doesn’t necessarily increase the moment ovulation occurs. It usually takes a few days for it to rise, and it typically peaks around 6-8 days post-Peak Fertility. 7. Can hormone levels vary from one luteal phase to another? Yes. Hormone levels naturally vary between cycles. Looking at trends across multiple cycles can provide a better understanding of what’s typical for your body than focusing on one cycle alone.

title: The contact center is no longer a cost center. It’s a growth engine.
summary: Most AI investments have improved efficiency, but not customer loyalty. Discover why leading enterprises are redesigning customer journeys around outcomes to drive retention, revenue, and long-term growth.
body_text: article The contact center is no longer a cost center. It’s a growth engine. Cailyn Michaan July 16, 2026 • 5 minutes Most enterprises have spent the last few years pouring money into AI for one goal: doing more with less. Deflect the ticket. Shorten the call. Route the conversation to whoever, or whatever, can close it fastest. That investment paid off in efficiency. It rarely paid off in loyalty. Customer expectations are moving faster than the operating models built to meet them, and the gap is starting to show. A contact center built to answer questions and close tickets can hit every efficiency target on the dashboard while customers quietly decide they’ve had enough. Efficient and effective are not the same thing, and CX leaders who are only measuring the first one are missing the second. The metric you’re optimizing for is the wrong one For a decade, contact centers have been graded on containment: how many conversations never reach a human, how many tickets close without escalation, how much cost gets removed per interaction. Those numbers look great in a board deck. They say almost nothing about whether the customer actually got what they came for. A closed ticket isn’t a loyal customer. A deflected conversation isn’t a solved problem. Most teams are still asking how to automate more. The leaders pulling ahead are asking a different question: how do we create better customer outcomes? That single shift in framing changes what gets built, what gets measured, and what gets reported to the CFO. Yesterday’s metric Tomorrow’s mandate Containment Retainment Efficiency Outcomes Answers Journeys The intent to shift is already there. In Gartner’s 2025 Customer Service Trends & Priorities Report , 51% of customer service and support leaders named increasing revenue through upselling or cross-selling to existing customers a key focus for the year. Most organizations have the will. Very few have an operating model built to deliver on it. Four things every customer outcome depends on Reframing success around outcomes sounds good in a strategy deck. Making it operational requires a model. LivePerson’s research points to four pillars that define whether a customer interaction actually resolves something, regardless of channel or whether AI or a human is on the other end: Go. Remove friction and get the customer to the right destination fast, without a maze of menus or transfers. Know. Deliver context-aware guidance that adapts as the conversation unfolds, not a script that ignores what the customer just said. Be heard. Capture intent, feedback, and signal in a way that actually improves the next interaction, not just this one. Do. Complete the task or transaction the customer came to complete, without punting them somewhere else to finish it. Most current AI deployments are strong on Go and Know. They answer questions and route conversations well. Far fewer are built to reliably Do, which is exactly where the value of orchestration over automation becomes visible. A bot that can explain a return policy is useful. A bot that can process the return is a growth engine. Gartner predicts that by 2029, agentic AI will autonomously resolve 80% of routine customer service issues without human intervention, a substantial jump from the basic conversational bots most deployments run on today, and projects that shift will cut operational costs by roughly 30%. That’s the Do pillar playing out at scale, and it’s the clearest sign yet that the real value shows up when AI moves beyond delivering information and starts enabling action. What separates the leaders from everyone else? The enterprises pulling ahead on CX aren’t rolling out more point solutions. They’re reinventing how the contact center works, and a few patterns show up consistently: They pick one high-value journey, something like onboarding, billing disputes, or renewals, and redesign it end-to-end instead of patching it channel by channel. They measure success in retention, revenue, and loyalty instead of containment rate. They build Go, Know, Be Heard, and Do into how the journey is designed from the start, rather than bolting automation onto an existing process. They redefine what their human agents are for, concentrating people on the moments that require complexity, emotion, and trust, and letting AI orchestrate everything around them. None of this is about which channel a customer prefers or how many bots are deployed. It’s about designing the outcome first and letting the technology serve it. Redesigning the journey means agents have to be ready for it Redesigning a journey around outcomes puts new demands on the people running it. An agent who’s used to reading from a script and closing tickets fast now has to exercise judgment, read intent, and complete a transaction under real pressure. That’s a different skill set, and it doesn’t show up on a quiz score. This is where readiness becomes part of the outcome equation, not a separate training initiative bolted on afterward. LivePerson’s Syntrix lets agents rehearse the exact kind of high-context, non-linear conversations that outcome-driven journeys demand, against realistic synthetic customers, before they ever reach a live one. Instead of confirming an agent memorized the policy, it confirms they can run the journey when a real customer goes off-script. Teams using it have cut ramp time by up to 30% and shortened bot testing cycles by 60%, which means the redesigned journey reaches customers faster and holds up once it gets there. If your organization is rethinking a journey around Go, Know, Be Heard, and Do, agent and AI readiness has to be part of that redesign from day one. The growth engine is being built now The contact center used to be the place where cost got managed. It’s becoming the place where lifetime value gets built, one journey at a time. The organizations that get there first won’t be the ones with the most automation. They’ll be the ones that redesigned what success means before their competitors did. The numbers back that up. Forrester found that 41% of customer-obsessed companies grew revenue by at least 10% in their last fiscal year, compared to just 10% of less mature companies, roughly a fourfold gap. Treating the contact center as a growth engine shows up on the balance sheet, not just in how leadership talks about CX. Ready to see what outcome-driven CX looks like in practice? title: Banking Payments Architecture, Real-Time Rails, AI, And Commercial Trends

body_text: Real-Time Payments, Orchestration Engines, And AI Fraud Detection Drive Capital Efficiencies Commercial banking is undergoing a structural metamorphosis, shifting from rigid, batch-processed legacy systems to a model of autonomous, event-native finance. The convergence of ISO 20022-native data fabrics and agentic AI is transforming payments from simple capital transfers into high-fidelity data signals that power real-time corporate decision-making. By leveraging sidecar cores and programmable liquidity, forward-thinking institutions are finally achieving the “always-on” agility required to support modern global supply chains — effectively turning the banking ledger into an intelligent, embedded engine for commercial growth. The architecture has evolved, but is the trust at scale there to activate these payments capabilities? This is the key trending payments issue that will unfold during the course of the year. Modern payment architecture trends are significantly reshaping cross-border, treasury, and B2B payments by reducing friction and increasing speed and transparency. Real-time and near-real-time rails, combined with ISO 20022 messaging, enable richer remittance data and faster reconciliation across borders, while cloud-native and API-driven platforms allow banks to integrate seamlessly with corporate enterprise resouce planning and treasury management systems. AI-enabled orchestration and smart routing help optimize payment paths based on cost, liquidity, and foreign-exchange exposure, improving working-capital efficiency for treasurers. Enhanced security models and standardized APIs make cross-border B2B payments more resilient and compliant, moving them closer to the speed, predictability, and user experience traditionally associated only with domestic payments. Tokenized Deposits And Digital Assets Spur 24/7 Transactions And Settlements The transition toward tokenized deposits and regulated digital assets is fundamentally rewriting the mechanics of commercial finance, shifting the industry from a world of “batch-processed” windows to one of autonomous, 24/7 settlement. By representing commercial banking money as digital tokens on a distributed ledger, financial institutions are bypassing the “weekend traps” and time-zone delays inherent in legacy correspondent banking. Digital payments innovations enable atomic settlement, where the exchange of value and its corresponding data happens simultaneously and instantaneously, ensuring that a payment is only finalized if the asset is delivered and vice versa. The integration of smart contracts allows for “programmable liquidity,” where payments are executed automatically upon the fulfillment of specific contractual conditions (e.g., a bill of lading being digitally signed). This always-on architecture effectively eliminates settlement risk and allows corporate treasurers to optimize their global balance sheets in real time, turning the banking ledger into a high-velocity engine for global commerce that never sleeps. Paul van der Merwe, head of enterprise architecture and director at Standard Bank Group in South Africa, states that innovations in core banking, payments, and compliance are now by nature built on the latest technology and are expected to handle real-time demands. Real-Time Payments Orchestration And Smart Routing The 2026 commercial banking landscape is defined by a shift toward autonomous, multirail liquidity. At the core is payment orchestration, an intelligent routing layer that acts as the “brain” for the enterprise, dynamically switching between domestic real-time rails (like FedNow and RTP) and global networks based on real-time cost-benefit analysis. While SWIFT continues to provide the standardized “common language” via ISO 20022, it has evolved into a bridge for central bank digital currencies and tokenized deposits, enabling the transition from traditional messaging to atomic settlement. In this new architecture, payments are no longer just financial transfers; they are programmable, data-rich events where settlement and reconciliation occur simultaneously. These instant payment rails allow global treasurers to move capital across borders with the same speed and finality as a domestic instant payment, effectively eliminating the “liquidity trap” of traditional cross-border windows. Aditya Singh, chief architect and director at Capital One, is seeing firsthand that when his team pairs AI and machine learning, they can automate process transformation and take a curated and controlled risk-on approach to innovation. title: What is an ESG Fund? Your 2022 Guide
summary: Diginex is a pioneering sustainability reporting technology company and advisory firm dedicated to helping organizations navigate the complexities of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) compliance and Supply chain Analysis. |
body_text: ‍ The amount of money flowing into socially responsible investing is growing at a very rapid rate. By the close of 2018, the total ESG investments stood at USD30.7 trillion. This figure is expected to shoot up further and reach USD50 trillion in the next 20 years. ESG investing funds are strong vehicles that help to target bonds and equities based on how the issuing firms work towards promoting sustainability. So, how well do you know ESG funds investing? Keep reading as we dig deeper to answer pertinent questions, including, “ what is an ESG fund ?” and “what are the best tips for selecting the right funds?” ‍ ‍ What is an ESG Fund? ESG funds are bonds and equity portfolios that prioritize ESG factors in the investment methodologies. They pick on the securities that come with high sustainability scores while excluding those with rampant ESG issues, such as poor records on pollution and labor relations. Investors use ESG sustainability reports from the featured companies as part of doing due diligence on the companies of interest. High ESG scores mean that the companies are not just focused on optimizing profits but also committed to helping the planet become a better place for all. What You Need to Know about ESG Sustainability ESG, shortening for environmental, social and governance, is a set of criteria that help gauge an organization’s commitment to helping the globe address challenges facing it. They ensure that the organizations are responsible in their operations to reduce negative impacts on the environment, use ethical leadership, and uphold fairness/ integrity in governance. Here is a closer look at the three pillars of ESG and their application in investment funds: Environmental: This is the first ESG pillar and it targets to help investors identify investments that aim at improving the planet. Some of the core areas of focus are minimizing carbon footprint and cutting down wastes. Social: This pillar assesses how companies manage relationships with staff, partners, and communities. For example, are the employees in the targeted organizations remunerated well? Other social considerations might include supporting courses for social justice and improving the well-being of the community. Governance: Organizations that put focus on ESG value always prioritize the shareholders. Therefore, they always use transparent processes and offer updates that shareholders can use to make important decisions. They are also governed properly and comply with laws of the jurisdictions hosting them. The Best Investment Approaches The next thing after answering the question “ what is an ESG fund?” is to identify the best investment approaches. Because ESG and ETF funds for investing can take different forms, from equities to bonds, there is no one-fits-all approach. So, here are some of the best approaches to consider: Restriction screening : ESG funds often opt out of organizations that are known to go against sustainability goals. So, you might want to check the fund with such screening for assurance against involvement in things like tobacco, firearms, and child labour. ESG integration : This is a hybrid approach employed for financial analysis to assess bonds and equities . This approach encourages investors to strike a 50/50 balance in the focus on financial and sustainability outlook . The good thing about ESG is that the concept has become an important part of organization management, with most companies releasing regular ESG audits for review by investors. Thematic engagement : This refers to an organization’s involvement in sectors that are dedicated to matters of ESG issues. Shareholder engagement : Involving shareholders directly can help to advance ESG investing. More companies are now roping them in to help craft ESG initiatives as a way of earning their trust and boosting revenue. Tips for Selecting the Best ESG Funds How do you identify the right ESG funds to invest in? It is important to have a good strategy for it, and the following four tips can help you narrow down to the best funds for better financial, environmental and social results. Set Out Clear Goals The first step is determining what you plan to achieve through ESG investing . Then, formalize them as the targeted investing goals. This can be very useful in defining the ESG investing strategy. Develop a Clear Plan to Achieve the Objectives Now, establish the amount of money that you want to use and the ESG factors of interest. Then, craft a plan to identify the environmental, social and governance (ESG) funds with assets that can align the capital at hand and companies that share your values. Therefore, it might be crucial to rethink what your priorities and targeted impact are. For example, what do you target with the etf funds? Should you focus on cutting down greenhouse gasses (GHG) as a method of addressing global warming or promoting biodiversity restoration? Diversify Your Investment As an investor, one of the rules of thumb is that you should never put all eggs in one basket. Therefore, you should look for the ESG mutual funds that spread funds as a method of risk management. If the fund has been in operation for some time, consider reviewing its recent performance. The insights can help to provide a clear idea of possible future sustainable performance of the selected companies in the months and years to come. Analyze Different Resources At this point, it is time to dive deeper into the selected ESG fund and the companies that support it. Here, you need to do a thorough analysis and identify the risks/ rewards of the fund. To avoid being biased, consider using multiple resources that provide info about the companies involved. Here are some of the main questions that you need to ask: What are the fees that should be paid for the fund? How do they compare to other funds? What specific criterion is employed by the fund when defining the portfolio holding? What areas do you desire the funds to be invested in? How does the fund discuss the ESG practices ? Talk to an Expert for Help Even with the tips we have listed above, many are those who find identifying the right ESG fund challenging. In such a situation, consider working with an expert for assistance to identify the right funds. Professionals can help you to understand how ESG funds work and the best funds to target. title: 6 signs your firm has outgrown Airtable as its source of truth
summary: Airtable rarely fails all at once. Here are 6 concrete signs your firm's operations have outgrown it and what to do.
body_text: Nobody wakes up one day and decides their Airtable setup needs to change. It's usually a slower thing. A base that used to feel tidy now has three "temporary" duplicate views nobody remembers creating. An automation stopped running after the workspace reached its monthly limit. Someone on the team is still copying numbers into a spreadsheet every Friday because two systems don't quite line up. None of that is a single breaking point. It's six or seven small signs stacking up, and by the time they're obvious, the firm has usually been living with the workaround for months without naming it. TL;DR Airtable's record limits scale from 1,000 on Free to 500,000+ on Enterprise Scale, but most firms don't hit the record ceiling first, they start running into operational limits: permissions, automations, and per-editor costs ( Airtable, 2026 ). Six concrete signs to check for: duplicated interfaces per client, climbing per-editor costs, automations quietly failing, permission workarounds, manual reconciliation between tools, and a growing list of "we'll fix that later" data fixes. Outgrowing Airtable doesn't have to mean leaving it. For many firms, the fix is keeping Airtable as the data layer and consolidating the operational layer, permissions, workflows, client access, on top of it. The right next step depends on how many of these signs you're seeing, not just one in isolation. What does it actually mean to outgrow Airtable? Outgrowing Airtable isn't about running out of storage. Airtable's record limits are generous enough that most professional services firms never hit them (see the table below). What actually happens is quieter: the base still holds the data fine, but the systems built around it, permissions, automations, client access, billing, start requiring more manual work than the team would like. Plan Records per base Automation runs / month Starting price Free 1,000 100 $0 Team 50,000 25,000 $20/editor/mo (annual) Business 125,000 100,000 $45/editor/mo (annual) Enterprise Scale 500,000+ 500,000 Custom For the full picture of what each plan includes and what triggers an upgrade, see our 2026 Airtable pricing breakdown . What are the 6 signs your firm has outgrown Airtable? 1. You're duplicating the same interface or view for every client Airtable Interfaces cap out at 50 per base. Long before firms hit that number, they've usually already built the habit of copying an interface, tweaking a filter, and calling it done for the next client. Each copy needs its own edits when the underlying process changes. If updating one field means updating it in fifteen places, that's usually a sign the setup could benefit from a different approach. We cover the mechanics of this specific cap in the Airtable automation limit nobody warns you about , which is often the sibling problem to interface duplication. 2. Your per-editor costs are climbing faster than your headcount Airtable bills per editor, and "editor" is defined broadly: a contractor who edits weekly, a finance reviewer who comments occasionally, a freelancer brought on for one engagement. All of them count as a full paid seat. Firms routinely discover, six months in, that they're paying for editors who log in once a month. That gradual cost increase if often one of the clearest signs the pricing model no longer matches how the team actually works. 3. You're spending more time checking whether automations are running Airtable's automation runs are capped by plan, and when the cap hits, automations pause until the limit resets or the workspace is upgraded, with no in-app warning next to the automation itself. Client onboarding sequences, invoice reminders, and status notifications can be missed until someone notices a workflow didn't happen as expected. If this sounds familiar, it's worth checking your current automation usage before it becomes an issue. 4. You're building workarounds instead of real permissions Airtable's sharing model was primarily designed for internal collaboration, not for showing 40 different clients 40 different slices of the same base. The common workaround, filtered views tied to a user's email, works up to a point, then breaks down as soon as you need field-level control (showing one client their project status but hiding your internal margin notes, for example). When the permission model requires this much manual scaffolding, the base is starting to stretch beyond its original strengths. 5. Someone is manually reconciling data between Airtable and 2 or 3 other tools This is the sign that costs the most time and shows up the least on any dashboard. A project management tool, an invoicing tool, and Airtable, each holding a piece of the same client record, not always perfectly in sync. According to Asana's Anatomy of Work Index (2026) , roughly 60% of the average workday already goes to work about work, communicating about tasks, hunting down information, and switching between apps, rather than the work itself. Manual reconciliation between tools is exactly the kind of task that index is describing, and it tends to fall on whoever is most conscientious on the team, often without anyone really noticing how much time it adds up to. 6. Your "we'll fix that later" list of data fixes keeps growing, not shrinking Every base accumulates a few of these: a field that should be a linked record but isn't, a status option that got renamed everywhere except in three old views, a duplicate table nobody's brave enough to delete. One or two of these is normal maintenance debt. A growing list that nobody has time to touch is a sign the base has more operational complexity than the team has bandwidth to manage inside Airtable's native tools alone. How many of these signs actually mean it's time to act? One sign on its own usually just means a cleanup task. Two or three, especially numbers 2, 3, and 5 together, usually mean the operational layer around Airtable is starting to outgrow what filtered views and native automations can carry, even if the data itself still fits comfortably inside the record limit. This is where it's worth being precise about what "outgrowing Airtable" actually requires. It doesn't require leaving Airtable. FD Works , for example, kept Airtable as their base and added a dedicated frontend on top specifically to improve the client-facing side of this equation. As Jonathan G, their team lead, put it: "Noloco enabled us to put a very professional frontend on top of our Airtable base." Redrock Entertainment shows the cost side of the same pattern. Their team had hit signs 1 and 2 directly: duplicated Airtable interfaces across more than 100 seats had, in their own words, "become a nightmare to manage," and every lightweight edit still required a full-priced editor seat. Redrock kept Airtable as the source of truth and added Noloco as the operating layer on top. "We've probably cut our annual software cost by about 60%," says Jesse VanDenKooy, Technology Solutions Architect at Redrock Entertainment. Same underlying move as FD Works, consolidating the operational layer rather than the data, just measured in the cost signs instead of the client-facing ones. What are the options once you've outgrown Airtable's operational layer? There are genuinely three paths, not two, and the right one depends on how much of the six signs above apply. Approach Best fit if Noloco Stay on Airtable alone Fewer than 2 of the 6 signs apply, and use is purely internal Not needed yet Keep Airtable as the data layer, add a frontend Signs 1, 3, or 4 apply: client access, permissions, or automations are the bottleneck, not the data itself Noloco connects directly to Airtable , adding branded portals, field-level permissions, and a dedicated workflow engine while your base stays exactly where it is Consolidate onto one operating system Signs 2, 5, and 6 apply: costs, reconciliation, and structural debt are all compounding across multiple tools Noloco can also serve as the primary database, retiring Airtable entirely or keeping it for a narrow, specific use case. See Noloco vs Airtable for a full side-by-side Firms rarely need to decide this in one leap. Most start in the middle row and only rethink their setup further once the reconciliation and cost signs (2, 5, 6) start outweighing the convenience of keeping Airtable as the single source of truth. For a broader look at what that consolidated setup looks like in practice, see consultancy management software: best tools in 2026 . Final thoughts Most teams don't outgrow Airtable overnight. It's usually a series of small operational signals that become more noticeable as the business grows. It's six small signs, duplicated interfaces, creeping seat costs, quiet automation failures, permission workarounds, manual reconciliation, and a growing backlog of data fixes, each one tolerable on its own, worth paying attention to together. The point isn't to panic at the first sign. It's to actually count how many apply, because that number, more than any single feature gap, is what tells you whether you need a cleanup afternoon or a real conversation about whether it's time to rethink the operational layer around your Airtable data. Frequently asked questions How many records can a single Airtable base hold? It depends on the plan: 1,000 on Free, 50,000 on Team, 125,000 on Business, and 500,000+ on Enterprise Scale ( Airtable, 2026 ). Most professional services firms hit operational limits, like automation runs or per-editor costs, before they hit the record ceiling. What's the difference between outgrowing Airtable and just needing more seats? Needing more seats is a straightforward upgrade. Outgrowing Airtable means the operational layer around it, permissions, automations, client access, requires ongoing manual workarounds that a plan upgrade doesn't fix. Do you have to migrate everything at once, or can Airtable stay for part of the operation? No single-cutover requirement exists. Many firms keep Airtable as the data layer and add a dedicated frontend on top first, only consolidating fully onto one system later if cost, reconciliation, or structural signs keep compounding. Is per-editor pricing the main reason firms move off Airtable? It's one of the most common reasons, particularly for firms with many occasional contributors, but it's rarely the only reason. It usually combines with automation limits, permission gaps, or reconciliation overhead. What's the actual first step in addressing these signs? Count how many of the six signs genuinely apply to your firm right now. One or two usually means a targeted fix. Three or more, especially cost, reconciliation, and automation failures together, usually means it's worth evaluating a dedicated operational layer. Does consolidating onto one system always mean giving up Airtable entirely? No. Some firms retire Airtable completely, others keep it for a narrow, specific use case (like a shared internal reference table) while others keep Airtable as the data layer and introduce a dedicated operational layer for workflows, permissions and client collaboration. title: The Lamborghini Portofino Concept Paved the Way for Chrysler’s Cab-Forward Aspirations
summary: The Chrysler LH platform was a major turning point for the automaker, an early ’90s coming-out party that proved it could build more than just K-car–derived econoboxes and minivans. The LH underpinned swoopy sedans like the Dodge Intrepid, Eagle Vision, and the upmarket Chrysler LHS, and the curvy charms of these family cars not only […]
body_text: The Chrysler LH platform was a major turning point for the automaker, an early ’90s coming-out party that proved it could build more than just K-car–derived econoboxes and minivans. The LH underpinned swoopy sedans like the Dodge Intrepid, Eagle Vision, and the upmarket Chrysler LHS, and the curvy charms of these family cars not only unlocked major sales success for the Pentastar as it left the financially shaky 1980s behind, they also sat well in showrooms beside equally striking models like the Dodge Viper roadster and the Dodge Ram pickup. (L-R) Chrysler Concorde, Dodge Intrepid, Eagle Vision Stellantis [ Editor’s note: After you’ve learned about the Portofino, check out Alex Kwanten’s deep dive on the LH platform . ] The design language expressed by these LH cars happens to have an unexpectedly exotic origin story. In fact, while the much-touted “cab forward” look found in Chrysler’s family of four-doors was born in the company’s Pacifica Design Center in San Diego, it had to make a detour to visit an Italian cousin on its passage into production. To untangle the web of the cab-forward design’s ancestry, we sat down with longtime Chrysler design chief Tom Gale, who played a pivotal role in shepherding the LH’s look from early-’80s clay model to global Lamborghini concept to ’90s mainstream sales success. Tom Gale Schicke/ullstein bild/Getty Images Out with the K, in with the Future “I just wanted to prove we weren’t brain-dead as far as design goes,” says Gale, referring to his approach when he took over the role of head of design at Chrysler in April 1985. At the time, the company had just emerged from fulfilling its loan repayment obligations, after the federal government had bailed it out of bankruptcy at the end of the previous decade—a financial reorganization that Chrysler had completed ahead of schedule largely thanks to the popularity of its cheap and cheerful K-platform commuter cars. Despite their popularity, it was clear the K-car party couldn’t go on forever, as there were definite limits to the looks and capabilities offered by these models. President Ronald Reagan and Lee Iacocca discuss the K-car platform. Bettmann Archive/Getty Images “What we were looking at was, what is the future of sedans?” Gale says. “Because the shape [of the K platform] was all too familiar. It came from a philosophy that was more comfortable with vinyl roofs and wire caps and white walls than the stuff of the future. We were really trying to figure out what is the most remarkable and effective way to package [a sedan]. And [we] were really trying to push the envelope.” Two designers—Kevin Verduyn and studio boss Tom Tremont—were spearheading the effort at Pacifica, where, Gale says, numerous design studies were underway to try to answer these questions. One pair stood out: the Mojave and the Navajo. The latter caught the eyes of Gale and Chrysler executive vice president Bob Lutz at a design review in 1986, and the clay model was brought to the company’s studios at Highland Park, where Verduyn and others continued to refine its look. “Kevin was just phenomenal. A great designer, a futurist, and a wonderful guy,” says Gale. It’s the future-focused nature of the Navajo that intrigued the design chief and proved it had potential to break Chrysler into a post-K-car future. Highland Park, by Way of Italy Lamborghini Portofino concept Stellantis It’s here that the cab-forward path skips across an ocean to engage in a little palace intrigue. In 1987, Chrysler purchased Lamborghini, a company that had spent much of the previous 10 years bouncing from one steward to another . It wasn’t clear exactly why the American automaker was so keen to add the beleaguered supercar builder to its portfolio, but the presence of Lamborghini under the same corporate banner offered an unexpected opportunity for Gale in terms of advancing the work that had been done so far on the Navajo. That chance came from a certain Chrysler executive vice president. “We had just bought Lamborghini … and we needed something to stir stuff up. And, of course, Bob was always a champion of stirring stuff up,” says Gale. Seeing the Navajo’s potential, Lutz threw his support behind building a full concept version, now renamed the Portofino, by way of the company’s international operations—specifically, Lamborghini. This allowed Gale to avoid significant amounts of budgetary and planning red tape back home. “Lamborghini really had nothing to do with the Portofino,” says Gale. “They were supplying the name and the conduit. It was a way of really attracting attention to something.” Lutz was able to ensure, too, that Chrysler’s design team retained control over the final version of the Portofino concept, something that was a sticking point with Lamborghini from day one. Stellantis “Lamborghini at the time, they were primarily using their designer there, the former Bertone guy, [Marcello] Gandini . He called the Portofino a potato, you know, because basically, if it wasn’t done by him, he didn’t like it. He wasn’t very tactful at all, and he was hard to deal with.” Interacting with Gandini’s team was so difficult that shortly after the Portofino concept was built, Chrysler’s management clashed with him over the design for the Countach replacement. Finding the Italian completely closed off to any suggestions from Chrysler, Gale ended up taking the Diablo back to Highland Park, completing the design, and then sending not just the completed blueprints but the full tooling model for the surface of the Diablo to Lamborghini. “I know that Lamborghini, being tight with Gandini, they would change it [otherwise]. I was content with being silent about it … and that never came out until the last few years, because nobody wanted to hear about Chrysler designing the Lamborghini,” says Gale. “I knew this was always going to be an argument, so I saved a photo book of the proposals that came about that were done in Highland Park.” Portofino’s Success Births a Cab-Forward Future AutoWeek/Crain Communications The Lamborghini Portofino concept debuted at the Frankfurt Motor Show in 1987, and it made considerable waves. It was built on the same bones as the Jalpa sports coupe and featured a high-revving V-8 engine, but looking back on it today, its influence on LH styling is crystal clear. Swap out the scissor doors and move the engine from the middle to the front of the sedan, and you’ve got a ringer for the original Dodge Intrepid. Dodge Intrepid model transparency Stellantis “Cab forward wasn’t just two words and a term. It was something you could see because it moved the A-pillar forward, it allowed the rear door to expand, and it allowed entry and exit to the car in a much different way,” says Gale. “From a packaging point of view, it became something real. It wasn’t just an advertising term.” Gale points out that the Portofino was “cab-forward on steroids,” primarily because it was a mid-engine car with short overhang at each end. And yet, despite its dramatic layout, much of the concept transferred into production, with even the Portofino’s greenish gold color and wheel design finding its way onto the Intrepid’s order sheet. Stellantis Dodge Intrepid ES Stellantis The Portofino endured long past the time when most concepts are put out to pasture, thanks to policy changes Gale made where concepts returned to the mothership at the end of their show career (rather than being dispersed to dealerships, collectors, or scrap heaps). An unfortunate fire during transport in 1991 nearly destroyed it completely, but instead of walking away from this important piece of its history, Chrysler used its insurance settlement to have California’s Metalcrafters rebuild it to an even higher spec—using real glass rather than the original Plexiglas for the greenhouse, for example. The vehicle remains in the company’s possession today. A Lasting Influence Stellantis Stellantis Lamborghini’s time under the Chrysler umbrella was brief, but there’s no question that using the supercar brand to birth the Portofino concept into the world paid massive dividends for the company’s more mainstream offerings, even if the bull badge was entirely superficial to the vehicle’s development. That wasn’t the only long-lasting gift that the Lamborghini concept bequeathed to the Pentastar, however. “The car was kind of a hit,” says Gale. “I really think it brought a lot of attention to Chrysler that was unexpected. And so (Chrysler CEO) [Lee] Iacocca asked the question, ‘If you can do concept cars like that, why can’t you do production cars?’ And I said, ‘Lee, we’ve been waiting for you to ask that question.’” View this post on Instagram A post shared by Chris Ashworth (@dtrockstar1) With Iacocca’s support, Gale was able to start a production design committee that tied in key executive management—manufacturing, planning, engineering, marketing—into the design process. Suddenly, the design department was on equal footing with the rest of the company’s approach to future planning, giving it a much stronger voice in how Chrysler brought cars to the market. How much of an impact did this have on the automaker’s fortunes? Take a look at the Chrysler of the 1980s and then contrast that against the much rowdier, risk-taking, and eye-catching efforts that emerged in the 1990s. Yes, the Lamborghini Portofino had a direct hand in the success of the LH cars—but its prominence on the international circuit also brought changes that introduced dynamic shapes like the Dodge Neon, the previously mentioned Ram and Viper, the Jeep Grand Cherokee, and the Plymouth Prowler and PT Cruiser, making the decade that followed perhaps the strongest in the company’s history. Tom Gale shows off concept cars at the North American International Auto Show, circa 2000. Clockwise from left: Dodge Viper GTS/R, Jeep Varsity, Dodge MAXXcab, and Chrysler 300 HEMI C. Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty Images The post The Lamborghini Portofino Concept Paved the Way for Chrysler’s Cab-Forward Aspirations appeared first on Hagerty Media .
